kid.question: What does the Lord say His people need to pay to be rescued?

options.text: A bag of silver
A flock of sheep
No money at all
A basket of grain

kid.explanation: The Lord promises redemption without money. The rescue is not something His people must buy.

kid.question: What message does the messenger bring to Zion?

options.text: Your city must surrender
Your journey ends here
Your enemies rule now
Your God is King

kid.explanation: The messenger announces peace and salvation and tells Zion that her God reigns.

kid.question: What do the watchmen do when the Lord restores Zion?

options.text: Run to the hills
Sing with one voice
Close the city gates
Gather for a meal

kid.explanation: The watchmen lift their voices and sing together when the Lord brings Zion again.

kid.question: Why can Jerusalem's ruined places rejoice?

options.text: The Lord has rescued Jerusalem
A king has built walls
An army has brought food
The people have found treasure

kid.explanation: The verse gives God's comfort and redemption of Jerusalem as the reasons for joy.

kid.question: How far will people see God's saving power?

options.text: Within Jerusalem's city walls
Throughout the whole earth
Across Egypt's river valley
Along Zion's mountain road

kid.explanation: Isaiah says all the ends of the earth will see God's salvation.

kid.question: What must those carrying the Lord's vessels be careful to do?

options.text: Keep themselves clean
Hide the vessels away
Trade the vessels quickly
Carry everything alone

kid.explanation: The people carrying the Lord's vessels are told to be clean and avoid unclean things.

kid.question: Who will protect the people as they leave?

options.text: The king of Egypt
The guards of Assyria
The watchmen of Babylon
The God of Israel

kid.explanation: The Lord will go before them and be their rearguard, protecting both ends of the journey.

kid.question: What does Isaiah say will happen to the Lord's servant?

options.text: He will be honored
He will be forgotten
He will become wealthy
He will escape abroad

kid.explanation: The servant will be exalted and lifted high. Isaiah describes honor rather than riches or escape.

kid.question: How do people treat the servant in Isaiah's description?

options.text: They choose him as king
They turn away from him
They welcome him with gifts
They follow him into battle

kid.explanation: The servant is despised and rejected; people hide their faces from him instead of honoring him.

kid.question: Whose griefs and wrongdoings does the servant bear?

options.text: Those of his children
Those of his teachers
Those of other people
Those of his ancestors

kid.explanation: The speakers say he carries our griefs and is wounded for our transgressions. His suffering benefits others.

high-school.question: How does the promise of redemption answer the account of oppression?

options.text: God requires Egypt to repay Israel
God restores people without demanding payment
God offers captives a commercial bargain
God transfers Israel to another ruler

high-school.explanation: After describing unpaid captivity and oppression, the Lord promises redemption without money and recognition of His name.

high-school.question: Why is the messenger's news followed by communal singing?

options.text: The messenger announces a military recruitment
God's reign brings comfort and restoration
The watchmen celebrate their new authority
The ruins become a profitable marketplace

high-school.explanation: The announcement that God reigns leads into watchmen singing and ruined Jerusalem rejoicing over redemption.

high-school.question: What does the image of the Lord's bare arm emphasize?

options.text: His work hidden inside the temple
His exhaustion after defending the city
His power displayed before the nations
His dependence upon a human army

high-school.explanation: The arm is bared in the sight of all nations, and the whole earth sees His salvation.

high-school.question: What combination characterizes the people's departure?

options.text: Personal purity with divine protection
Urgent flight with military protection
Secret travel with priestly disguises
Public celebration with foreign escorts

high-school.explanation: The people must be clean, but they need not flee in haste because God goes before and behind them.

high-school.question: Which contrast shapes the portrait of the servant?

options.text: His disfigurement alongside his coming exaltation
His royal clothing alongside his poverty
His military victories alongside his losses
His youthful beauty alongside his aging

high-school.explanation: The servant is promised exaltation, yet his appearance is marred; the juxtaposition challenges an ordinary picture of honor.

high-school.question: Why do the kings stop speaking in the servant passage?

options.text: They encounter something previously unheard
They surrender their crowns to Zion
They receive instructions to remain silent
They forget their own national languages

high-school.explanation: The verse connects their silence with seeing what they had not been told and considering what they had not heard.

high-school.question: How does the plant imagery help explain the servant's reception?

options.text: His beginnings promise immediate public acclaim
His growth depends on a fertile kingdom
His beginnings lack the appeal people expect
His growth separates him from ordinary hardship

high-school.explanation: A tender plant and root in dry ground are followed by the statement that his appearance does not attract people.

high-school.question: Which judgment about the servant does the passage begin to overturn?

options.text: His suffering means the people admire him
His sorrow means his service has ended
His sorrow means the enemy has repented
His suffering means God has rejected him

high-school.explanation: The people esteem him smitten by God, yet the speaker says he has been carrying their griefs and sorrows.

high-school.question: What is the relationship between the servant's wounds and the people?

options.text: His suffering makes them lose their freedom
His wounds show them how to fight
His wounds announce their coming military defeat
His suffering brings them healing and peace

high-school.explanation: The text connects his wounds to our transgressions and his stripes to our healing, giving the suffering a redemptive purpose.

high-school.question: How do the two verses expand the promise of salvation?

options.text: Jerusalem's restoration remains confined to its own residents
Jerusalem's restoration becomes visible throughout the earth
Jerusalem's comfort becomes dependent on neighboring kings
Jerusalem's comfort replaces the need for divine action

high-school.explanation: The comfort and redemption of Jerusalem are followed by salvation seen at all the ends of the earth.

expert.question: What does the repeated idea of being taken for nothing establish?

options.text: Oppression supplies no rightful claim over God's people
Oppression creates a debt Israel must repay abroad
Redemption depends upon an agreed price between rulers
Redemption compensates the captors for their lawful ownership

expert.explanation: Being sold for nothing and taken away for nothing undercut the captors' claim; the Lord's redemption does not require a purchase price.

expert.question: How does the promised knowledge of God's name answer the preceding complaint?

options.text: Public dishonor gives way to recognition of His voice
Public dishonor gives way to adoption of foreign names
The people's howling becomes a command to silence prophets
The people's oppression becomes proof that God has withdrawn

expert.explanation: The complaint that God's name is blasphemed is answered by the promise that His people will know His name and recognize the speaker.

expert.question: Which movement organizes the announcement's widening audience?

options.text: Nations to watchmen to messenger to ruins
Ruins to messenger to nations to watchmen
Messenger to watchmen to ruins to nations
Watchmen to nations to ruins to messenger

expert.explanation: The sequence moves from one herald to watchmen, Jerusalem's ruins, and finally all nations and the ends of the earth.

expert.question: How do the consecutive verses distribute responsibility for the departure?

options.text: The people secure passage; God cleans their vessels
The carriers provide weapons; the watchmen provide holiness
The carriers remain behind; the other travelers flee
The people maintain purity; God secures their passage

expert.explanation: The command to be clean concerns the travelers, while God provides the advance guard and rearguard that remove the need for haste.

expert.question: What expectation does the ordering of exaltation and disfigurement unsettle?

options.text: Honor must follow an extended period of public silence
Honor must correspond to an impressive outward appearance
Prudence must require a withdrawal from national affairs
Prudence must arise from a life free of suffering

expert.explanation: The promise that the servant will be high is immediately juxtaposed with his marred appearance, disrupting an equation of honor with visible splendor.

expert.question: What is the stated basis for the kings' astonished silence?

options.text: New recognition beyond their previous reports
Recognition of their own political success
A prohibition imposed by the messenger
A confession demanded by the watchmen

expert.explanation: The explanatory clause says they see what had not been told and consider what they had not heard.

expert.question: How do the opening question and growth imagery work together?

options.text: They frame a royal succession confirmed by attractive appearance
They equate universal belief with plentiful agricultural growth
They frame a revelation that lacks expected outward appeal
They equate failed testimony with the absence of revelation

expert.explanation: The question about belief introduces a servant whose tender growth and unappealing appearance do not meet ordinary expectations of greatness.

expert.question: What reversal occurs in the speakers' assessment of the servant?

options.text: The honored leader is recognized as causing their griefs
The dismissed sufferer is recognized as carrying their burdens
The rejected stranger is recognized as avoiding their sorrows
The admired teacher is recognized as concealing divine judgment

expert.explanation: They first esteem him not and regard him as smitten by God, while the confession identifies the griefs and sorrows as their own.

expert.question: What gives the verse's repeated first-person plurals their interpretive force?

options.text: They connect his suffering with his private guilt and recovery
They connect his suffering with the speakers' guilt and healing
They identify the wounds as injuries shared equally by enemies
They identify the peace as a treaty negotiated by kings

expert.explanation: Our transgressions, our iniquities, our peace, and we are healed consistently place the benefits and guilt with the speakers.

expert.question: Which reading best accounts for both halves of the servant portrait?

options.text: Exaltation replaces suffering before the people's wrongdoing is addressed
Disfigurement proves the servant's honor was a mistaken prediction
Rejection proves the servant suffers solely for his own wrongdoing
Exaltation accompanies suffering that benefits those who reject him

expert.explanation: The servant's exaltation in 52:13 stands alongside rejection and wounds for others in 53:3-5; neither theme can simply cancel the other.
